clue.text: Admiralty finally rearms bombs around old warship

indicators.note: to sit around something is to surround it, so one piece encloses another
something that bombs explodes, blowing the letters apart to land in a new order
finally points to the closing letter of the word it follows

parts.note: last letter of Admiralty
taken as written
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: The navy brass rearm an old warship that is being bombed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Y and the letters of 'rearms' are scrambled together into MARYRSE, then O is slipped in to give MARY ROSE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mary Rose was Henry VIII's flagship, which sank in 1545 and was raised from the Solent in 1982.

clue.text: Your escort engages government department

indicators.note: to engage something is to take it in or hold it, so one piece grips the other inside

parts.note: a beau is a male companion who escorts a woman
UR is the text-message spelling of your

explanation.surface: A personal escort is apparently employed by some government department.
explanation.walkthrough: UR as a spelling of 'your' comes from text messaging; the escort is the outer piece even though it is named second.
explanation.definitionFit: A bureau is an office or agency of state, such as the Federal Bureau of Investigation in America.

clue.text: Displaying bottle, United supporter overturned attack

parts.note: U is the usual abbreviation for United in team names

indicators.note: something overturned is turned upside down, and in a down light that runs its letters backwards

parts.note: a fan supports a team
a raid is a sudden attack

explanation.surface: A Manchester United fan, holding a bottle, is knocked over in a football brawl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottle' is British slang for courage or nerve, not a container; displaying bottle means showing pluck.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing nerve or courage is the same as being fearless, so displaying bottle is a slangy synonym for brave.

clue.text: Triumphant cry of 'Mistake!' rued, retracted to an extent

indicators.note: to retract is to draw back, so the letters are read in the backward direction
only to an extent means only partly, so just a portion of the words is used

parts.note: the tail of Mistake runs into rued

explanation.surface: Someone regretfully takes back their shout that something was a mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: Read backwards, the letters straddling 'Mistake' and 'rued' spell EUREKA.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes supposedly shouted it on discovering displacement in his bath, and it remains the classic exclamation of discovery and success.

clue.text: Standing of data science around university

indicators.note: lying around something means surrounding it, so one piece wraps the other

parts.note: stats, short for statistics, is the science of data
U is the standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: The prestige data science now enjoys in academia.
explanation.walkthrough: STATS holds U to give STATUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing and status both mean a person's position or rank relative to others in society or a profession.

clue.text: State checks exposed financial reserves for 24 hours

indicators.note: to check something is to hold it in, so one piece restrains the other inside

parts.note: to state something is to say it

indicators.note: exposed means stripped of its covering, so the outside letters are removed

parts.note: funds, with its first and last letters removed

explanation.surface: A government audits bank reserves that were exposed as short for a whole day.
explanation.walkthrough: Financial reserves are funds; 'exposed' strips the outer letters, and the definition works by example, since any day lasts 24 hours.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunday is one particular day of the week, and a day lasts twenty-four hours, so this definition is by example.

clue.text: Book every twelve months

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a yearbook, especially a children's one tied to a comic or TV show
second meaning: happening once a year

explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb meaning reserve, as if booking something yearly; here it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain a hardback gift edition published yearly is called this, and the adjective means yearly or recurring each year.

clue.text: Not much time left to open low-calorie beer

indicators.note: to open something you get inside it, so these letters push into the middle of the other piece

parts.note: lite is the commercial spelling for a light, low-calorie beer
T is the abbreviation for time
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: With little time remaining, someone cracks open a light beer.
explanation.walkthrough: T and L go into LITE, between the T and the E, giving LITTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases describe a small quantity or amount, as in having little money or not much money.

clue.text: Questionable climber atop rocks

indicators.note: to rock is to shake about, so these letters are jolted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dubious mountaineer perches on top of some rocks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocks' sits in the scene as the crag being climbed, but works as a verb meaning shakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Something open to doubt or dispute is hard to resolve, so questionable and difficult to settle mean much the same.

clue.text: Unfortunately, enemy hides unknown catalyst

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it tucked inside, so one piece conceals the other
an unfortunate outcome is a mishap, so these letters end up disordered

parts.note: taken as written
in algebra x, y and z are the unknowns

explanation.surface: A worrying military report: the enemy is concealing some mystery trigger.
explanation.walkthrough: ENEMY is rearranged to ENYME, which takes in Z to make ENZYME.
explanation.definitionFit: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions in living organisms without being consumed, the biological type of catalyst.

clue.text: Throws back Republican votes for introducing force

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican

indicators.note: to introduce is literally to lead into, so one piece is brought inside another

parts.note: to elect is to vote someone in
F is the symbol for force in physics

explanation.surface: A Republican vetoes something by voting for a bill that brings in force.
explanation.walkthrough: R is followed by ELECTS, and F is introduced after its first letter: R plus E-F-LECTS.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirror or a surface reflects light or sound by bouncing it back, which is throwing it back.

clue.text: Villain, one in the past

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one
ago means back in the past

explanation.surface: A wicked character who belongs to history.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a description of a former baddie; the answer is a specific one from the stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Iago is the scheming ensign in Shakespeare's Othello, often called one of the greatest stage villains ever written.

clue.text: Excellent but anal eccentric burying live rodents, essentially

indicators.note: to bury something is to put it deep inside, so one piece goes into the other
eccentric means off-centre and odd, so these letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the essence of a word is its core, so the central letter is taken

parts.note: the fourth of seven letters sits at the centre
to live is to be, to exist

explanation.surface: A fussy, obsessive oddball keeps live rodents buried, yet is somehow excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Anal' is the colloquial short form of anal-retentive, meaning obsessively fussy, but here it is just letters; 'essentially' means the heart of 'rodents'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that cannot be beaten or bettered is outstanding, so unbeatable works as an emphatic synonym for excellent.

clue.text: Brilliant! Again paid out grant charges

parts.note: re- is the prefix meaning again

indicators.note: to charge is to load or fill, so one piece is packed inside another

parts.note: money paid out has been spent
to grant someone something temporarily is to lend it

explanation.surface: Delight at receiving another grant payment, or at fees being repaid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' looks like a noun for fees but is a verb meaning loads; 'Brilliant!' looks like an exclamation but defines a word for shining.
explanation.definitionFit: Resplendent means dazzling or gloriously shining, matching brilliant in its visual sense rather than its exclamatory one.

clue.text: Sanctimonious rogues protecting soldiers who'll goad animals

definitions.note: a relative clause standing in for a plural noun: those who will goad animals

parts.note: pi is informal British for pious or sanctimonious

indicators.note: to protect something is to shield it all round, so one piece surrounds the other

parts.note: a cad is a dishonourable man, a rogue
OR stands for Other Ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Smug villains shield troops who are going to bait some beasts.
explanation.walkthrough: OR, for Other Ranks, is the usual crossword soldiers; 'soldiers who'll goad animals' reads as one phrase, but the definition starts after 'soldiers'.
explanation.definitionFit: Picadors are mounted bullfighters who jab the bull with lances to weaken and provoke it before the matador's turn.

clue.text: Devil close to ensnaring large English Dickensian protagonist

indicators.note: to ensnare is to trap something inside, so letters are caught within a pair of outer pieces

parts.note: Old Nick is a name for the Devil
by means near or close to
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Satan, near enough, trapping a big Englishman out of a Dickens novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' is not an indicator but a piece: NICK and BY together ensnare L and E.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicholas Nickleby is the title character and hero of Charles Dickens's third novel, published in monthly parts in 1838–39.

clue.text: Identify digit

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to point out a culprit to the police
second meaning: one of the five on a hand

explanation.walkthrough: 'Digit' suggests a number to be identified; here it is a part of the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: To finger someone is slang for informing on or pointing out a suspect, and the noun names any of the hand's digits.

clue.text: Discipline son Henry amidst calm

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son

indicators.note: amidst means in the middle of, so one piece is set inside another

parts.note: cool means calm and composed
H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: A parent quietly tells off a son called Henry without losing their temper.
explanation.walkthrough: S comes first, then H sits inside COOL after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: As verbs both mean to train or drill someone in good habits; as nouns both mean a field of study.

clue.text: Following encryption, mail hacker successfully

indicators.note: encryption scrambles a message into code, so once encrypted these letters appear in another order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cybercriminal breaks into encrypted email without a hitch.
explanation.walkthrough: The computer setting makes 'mail hacker' look like the subject, but these ten letters are just the material to be scrambled.
explanation.definitionFit: Working like a charm is an idiom for going perfectly, as if by magic, so it means with complete success.

clue.text: Base jokes causing fits

parts.note: e is the base of natural logarithms
quips are witty jokes

explanation.surface: Crude humour sends people into fits of laughter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like an adjective for vulgar and 'fits' like bouts of laughter; really base is the mathematical constant and fits means kits out.
explanation.definitionFit: To fit out a ship or expedition is to supply it with gear, so fits in this sense means provides or furnishes.

clue.text: Old country mum caught hen?

parts.note: ma is an informal word for mother

indicators.note: to catch words is to hear them, so the answer is what the ear picks up

parts.note: a hen is a layer of eggs, hence the question mark

explanation.surface: Mother has caught a chicken, perhaps on an old farm abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' looks like a capture but means heard: 'ma layer' in a non-rhotic British accent sounds like MALAYA. The question mark flags a hen defined as a layer.
explanation.definitionFit: Malaya was the British colony and later federation on the Malay Peninsula that became part of Malaysia in 1963.

clue.text: Caught initially abusing cocaine and heroin

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letters are kept

parts.note: first letter of Caught
first letter of abusing
first letter of cocaine
first letter of and

explanation.surface: A drug user is arrested for taking cocaine and heroin together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cocaine' looks like part of the definition alongside heroin, but it only supplies a first letter; 'heroin' alone is defined.
explanation.definitionFit: Caca is recorded street slang for heroin, a drug-culture term rather than an everyday one.

clue.text: Fresh idea involving celebrated revolutionary part of Mass

indicators.note: a revolution is a turning round, so the letters are spun to run backwards
to involve is to enfold or include, so one piece takes another inside
a fresh version is a new one, so these letters are made over in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
something celebrated is praised, as in sung of

explanation.surface: A new notion about a famous rebel figure in the Catholic liturgy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' suggests a political rebel such as Che, but it is only the turning signal, and the animal that results is a wildebeest.
explanation.definitionFit: The Agnus Dei, Latin for Lamb of God, is a prayer said or sung in the Roman Catholic liturgy before communion.

clue.text: Lounge suite picked up after losing online address

indicators.note: after losing something you no longer have it, so those letters are taken out
to pick up a word is to hear it, so the spelling follows the sound

parts.note: the furniture word is pronounced like sweet, and a lollipop is a sweet
an IP address identifies a device on the internet

explanation.surface: A sofa set bought on the web, collected once its website listing was taken down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lounge suite' reads as a sofa set, but 'Lounge' is the definition and 'suite' is heard as sweet: LOLLIPOP minus IP is LOLLOP.
explanation.definitionFit: To lollop is to lounge or loll about lazily, though it more often means to move in an ungainly bounding way.

clue.text: Statement withdrawing recurring theme, right

indicators.note: to withdraw is to draw back, so the letters are pulled backwards

parts.note: a trope is a recurring motif or theme
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A public statement backing away from a theme it has repeated, and rightly so.
explanation.walkthrough: TROPE and R together are reversed, so the R that ends the clue leads the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A report is an account or announcement giving information, which is a formal kind of statement.

clue.text: Sign as percussion instrument delivered

indicators.note: a speech is delivered when it is spoken, so the answer is how the words are said

parts.note: a cymbal is a brass plate struck in a drum kit or orchestra

explanation.surface: A gong or drum handed over as a signal of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivered' suggests a parcel handed over; it means spoken, giving a word that sounds the same as the instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A symbol is a mark or figure that stands for something else, so a sign in the sense of an emblem or token.
